item.title: “Suppose, monks, a fisherman throws a baited hook into a deep lake. A fish, seeing the bait, swallows the hook. Thus, monks, that fish, having…
item.description:
“Suppose, monks, a fisherman throws a baited hook into a deep lake. A fish, seeing the bait, swallows the hook. Thus, monks, that fish, having swallowed the fisherman’s hook, has fallen into misfortune, into calamity, subject to the fisherman’s will. So too, monks, there are these six hooks in the world, leading to the misfortune of beings, to the calamity of living beings. What six? Monks, there are forms cognizable by the eye that are desirable, agreeable, pleasant, charming, connected with sensuality, enticing. If a monk delights in those forms, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — then that monk is called one who has swallowed Māra’s hook, has fallen into misfortune, into calamity, subject to the Evil One’s will. There are sounds … odors … tastes … touches … phenomena cognizable by the mind that are desirable … enticing. If a monk delights in those phenomena, praises them, and dwells with lust for them — then that monk is called one who has swallowed Māra’s hook, has fallen into misfortune, into calamity, subject to the Evil One’s will.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.230

item.title: “Seeing the destruction of birth, The end of fetters, Destroying the path of sensual desire, Without remainder — That one is pure, faultless, Stainless, undefiled…
item.description:
“Seeing the destruction of birth,
The end of fetters,
Destroying the path of sensual desire,
Without remainder —
That one is pure, faultless,
Stainless, undefiled —
The Tathāgata is worthy of offerings.”

“One who does not see a self within the self,
Concentrated, upright, steady,
Without desire, without rigidity, without doubt —
The Tathāgata is worthy of offerings.”

“One in whom there is no root of delusion,
Who knows, who sees all things,
Who bears this last body —
Attaining perfect enlightenment,
The unsurpassed state of peace —
Thus is the Tathāgata, worthy of offerings.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 3.4

item.title: “‘Empty is the world, empty is the world,’ venerable sir, is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is it said that the world is empty?”…
item.description:
“‘Empty is the world, empty is the world,’ venerable sir, is said. To what extent, venerable sir, is it said that the world is empty?” - “Ānanda, because the world is empty of self and anything belonging to self, therefore it is said that the world is empty. And what, Ānanda, is empty of self and anything belonging to self? The eye, Ānanda, is empty of self and anything belonging to self. Forms are empty of self and anything belonging to self. Eye-consciousness … Eye-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on eye-contact … that feeling is empty of self and anything belonging to self. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind … Phenomena … Mind-consciousness … Mind-contact … Whatever feeling arises dependent on mind-contact … that feeling is empty of self and anything belonging to self. And because it is empty of self and anything belonging to self, Ānanda, it is said that the world is empty.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.85

item.title: “And what, monks, is the practice of calming? Here, monks, a monk does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, calms, ends, and…
item.description:
“And what, monks, is the practice of calming? Here, monks, a monk does not consent to arisen sensual thought; he abandons, dispels, calms, ends, and makes it non-existent. He does not consent to arisen ill-will thought … harmful thought … to arisen evil, unwholesome thoughts; he abandons, dispels, calms, ends, and makes them non-existent. This, monks, is called the practice of calming.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.164
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, then I dwelt heedful, ardent, resolute. When a sensual thought arose, I understood: ‘This sensual thought has arisen in me, and it leads to…
item.description:
“Monks, then I dwelt heedful, ardent, resolute. When a sensual thought arose, I understood: ‘This sensual thought has arisen in me, and it leads to my own harm, to others’ harm, to the harm of both, destroys wisdom, is part of vexation, does not lead to Nibbāna.’ Monks, as I reflected: ‘This sensual thought leads to my own harm’ – it subsided. As I reflected: ‘It leads to others’ harm’ – it subsided. As I reflected: ‘It leads to the harm of both’ – it subsided. As I reflected: ‘It destroys wisdom, is part of vexation, does not lead to Nibbāna’ – it subsided. Thus, monks, I continued to remove, abandon, and put an end to sensual thoughts.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 19 – Dvedhāvitakkasutta

item.title: “So too, monks, a monk reflecting thus gains great benefit in wholesome states. ‘Do I dwell much with greed? Do I dwell much without greed?…
item.description:
“So too, monks, a monk reflecting thus gains great benefit in wholesome states. ‘Do I dwell much with greed? Do I dwell much without greed? Do I dwell much with a mind of ill-will? Do I dwell much with a mind without ill-will? Do I dwell much overcome by sloth and torpor, or do I dwell much with sloth and torpor abandoned? Do I dwell much with restlessness, or do I dwell much without restlessness? Do I dwell much with doubt, or do I dwell much with doubt overcome? Do I dwell much with anger, or do I dwell much without anger? Do I dwell much with a defiled mind, or do I dwell much with an undefiled mind? Do I dwell much with bodily fever, or do I dwell much without bodily fever? Do I dwell much with laziness, or do I dwell much with energy and striving? Do I dwell much unconcentrated, or do I dwell much concentrated?’”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.51
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: Thoughts of lust Are the sensual pleasures of humans, The beautiful things in the world Are not themselves sensual pleasures. Thoughts of lust Are the…
item.description:
Thoughts of lust
Are the sensual pleasures of humans,
The beautiful things in the world
Are not themselves sensual pleasures.
Thoughts of lust
Are the sensual pleasures of humans.
The beautiful things remain
As they are in the world,
But the wise here
Subdue their lust.

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.63

item.title: “If anyone speaks of ‘a heap of the unwholesome,’ monks, he would speak rightly of the five hindrances. Indeed, the entire heap of the unwholesome,…
item.description:
“If anyone speaks of ‘a heap of the unwholesome,’ monks, he would speak rightly of the five hindrances. Indeed, the entire heap of the unwholesome, monks, is just the five hindrances. What five? The hindrance of sensual desire, the hindrance of ill-will, the hindrance of sloth and torpor, the hindrance of restlessness and remorse, the hindrance of doubt. If anyone speaks of ‘a heap of the unwholesome,’ he would speak rightly of the five hindrances. Indeed, the entire heap of the unwholesome is just the five hindrances.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 5.52

item.title: Elder Rādha: As rain seeps into a house with a faulty roof, So lust seeps into an undeveloped mind. As rain does not seep into…
item.description:
Elder Rādha:

As rain seeps into a house with a faulty roof,
So lust seeps into an undeveloped mind.

As rain does not seep into a house with a good roof,
So lust does not seep into a well-developed mind.

From: Theragāthā 2.7
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, whatever a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon, that becomes the inclination of his mind. Monks, if a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon…
item.description:
“Monks, whatever a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon, that becomes the inclination of his mind. Monks, if a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon sensual thoughts, he has abandoned thoughts of renunciation. When his mind has become heavy with sensual thoughts, his mind inclines to sensual thoughts. Monks, if a monk frequently thinks and ponders upon thoughts of ill-will … thoughts of harmfulness, he has abandoned thoughts of non-harmfulness. When his mind has become heavy with harmful thoughts, his mind inclines to harmful thoughts.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 19 – Dvedhāvitakkasutta
